questions.stem: Consider the claim: 'Any central atom with three sigma bonds must be sp2.' Given BF3: three B–F sigma bonds, zero boron lone pairs, planar; NH3: three N–H sigma bonds, one nitrogen lone pair, pyramidal. Decide whether these observations support the claim, give the decisive warrant, and state a more defensible introductory rule. Explain what the shape observations alone do not prove about orbitals.

answer.summary: The observations do not support the claim. BF3 and NH3 each have three central sigma bonds, but NH3 also has a lone-pair domain. The decisive introductory warrant is total local electron-domain count, not sigma-bond count alone: for common small main-group localized examples, 2/3/4 domains are described as sp/sp2/sp3. BF3 is therefore the three-domain case, whereas NH3 is the four-domain case. Observed shape can motivate or test such a model, but shape alone is not direct proof that particular atomic orbitals literally hybridised.

questions.stem: A student says, 'If the electron-domain geometry is tetrahedral, the atoms must form a tetrahedral molecular shape.' Evaluate the statement using CH4, NH3 and H2O, with their respective central lone-pair counts of zero, one and two.

answer.summary: The statement is false. CH4, NH3 and H2O each have four central electron domains and therefore tetrahedral electron-domain geometry in VSEPR. CH4 has 0 lone pairs, so four bonded atoms form a tetrahedral molecular shape; NH3 has 1 lone pair, so three bonded atoms form a trigonal-pyramidal shape; H2O has 2 lone pairs, so two bonded atoms form a bent shape. Electron-domain geometry includes lone pairs; molecular shape names the atom positions.
